info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 3.3: Building the Manifest and Binding It to TEI.

name.text: 01 Question: What Today Produces

questiontext.text: What does the bidirectional coordinate binding created in Lesson 3.3 enable for a digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Today's artefact links each transcribed line to the exact region of parchment it transcribes, in both directions and machine-actionably.

answer.text: A reader can click any transcribed line to view the exact parchment region, or select a manuscript region to view its transcription, making evidence machine-actionable.

feedback.text: Correct. Coordinate binding links text to image in both directions, making every reading immediately verifiable against its physical evidence.

answer.text: It automatically translates Greek verse into rhyming English poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The binding links transcription lines to image coordinates; it does not generate poetic translations.

answer.text: It compiles the digital edition into a physical print book using an automated printing press.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It builds a web-accessible, machine-actionable digital link between text and evidence.

answer.text: It locks the digital edition behind a paywall to monetize access to manuscript scans.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The binding creates open, interactive scholarly links between text and evidence.

name.text: 02 Question: Two Manifests, Two Situations

questiontext.text: In 'Situation B' (authoring your own IIIF manifest for your passage), what is your relationship to the image files?

generalfeedback.text: Authoring a manifest does not mean hosting images — you describe an object that references the institution's Image API endpoints.

answer.text: You author a JSON-LD manifest describing the object and its sequence, but the images remain hosted and served by the holding institution's Image API endpoints.

feedback.text: Correct. Authoring a manifest does not mean hosting images yourself; you describe the object and reference existing Image API endpoints.

answer.text: You must download all master TIFFs and host them on a private dedicated physical server in your home.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Situation B references external institutional Image API endpoints without hosting image files.

answer.text: You take legal ownership of the physical manuscript codex and its copyright.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Authoring a digital manifest has no effect on legal ownership of physical objects.

answer.text: You re-photograph the original manuscript in the library reading room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You construct a manifest referencing existing digital images.

name.text: 03 Question: Recording Canvas Identifiers

questiontext.text: Why is it essential to record both canvas dimensions (height, width) and image dimensions (body.height, body.width) when surveying folios?

generalfeedback.text: Record canvas ids, canvas dimensions, and image dimensions together — where the last two differ, every coordinate needs scaling.

answer.text: Canvas dimensions define the coordinate space for annotations; if image dimensions differ from canvas dimensions, all computed coordinates require scaling.

feedback.text: Correct. If canvas and image pixel dimensions differ, coordinates calculated from image pixels will be systematically offset unless scaled.

answer.text: If canvas dimensions are recorded, web browsers will refuse to display text fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Canvas dimensions establish the 2D coordinate space for annotations and images.

answer.text: Image dimensions must match canvas dimensions down to the nanometer under international treaty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mismatches are common technical variations that require simple proportional scaling.

answer.text: Recording image dimensions is only required for manuscripts written after the invention of print.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coordinate scaling applies to all digital surrogates regardless of date.

name.text: 04 Question: Determining Coordinates for a Region

questiontext.text: Why does Lesson 3.3 require students to measure and bind a few lines by hand rather than relying entirely on automated tools?

generalfeedback.text: Bind a few regions by hand today so that you can verify next week's automated line coordinates against a known-good case.

answer.text: Hand-measured coordinates provide an understood, known-good control against which next week's automated HTR line coordinates can be verified for scaling or offset errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Having a hand-verified ground truth allows immediate detection of systematic scaling or translation errors in automated transforms.

answer.text: Automated HTR tools are strictly forbidden by TEI Consortium licensing regulations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR and automated layout analysis are central tools introduced in Week 4.

answer.text: Hand measurement is the only way to generate XML files that pass RelaxNG validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation checks XML syntax and schema conformance, not the method of measurement.

answer.text: Computer algorithms cannot calculate pixel coordinates on 2D images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms calculate coordinates rapidly; hand measurement provides a reliable control.

name.text: 05 Question: The TEI Facsimile Module

questiontext.text: How do the core elements of the TEI <facsimile> module map conceptually to IIIF Presentation API entities?

generalfeedback.text: <facsimile> describes surfaces and zones separately from the transcription, and TEI <surface> maps to a IIIF canvas.

answer.text: <facsimile> corresponds to the Manifest, <surface> maps to a Canvas, and <zone> corresponds to a canvas coordinate region (fragment selector).

feedback.text: Correct. TEI models a physical writing surface (IIIF Canvas), and models a bounded region on that surface.

answer.text: <facsimile> represents a SQL database, <surface> represents an audio recording, and <zone> represents a CSS font.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI facsimile elements model physical documents and their digital spatial surrogates.

answer.text: <surface> represents an individual word, while <zone> represents the entire library building.

feedback.text: Incorrect. represents a page/canvas; represents a sub-region (line/block/word).

answer.text: <facsimile> is restricted to modern photographs, while IIIF is restricted to handwritten parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both TEI facsimile and IIIF apply across all historical and modern documents.

name.text: 06 Question: Two Coordinate Conventions

questiontext.text: What is the key geometric difference between TEI <zone> coordinate attributes (ulx, uly, lrx, lry) and a IIIF fragment selector (#xywh=x,y,w,h)?

generalfeedback.text: TEI names two corners and IIIF names a corner plus dimensions; treating IIIF's last two values as a corner produces regions that are too large.

answer.text: TEI specifies two opposite diagonal corner points (upper-left and lower-right), whereas IIIF specifies one corner point (x,y) plus width and height.

feedback.text: Correct. TEI defines opposite corners (ulx/uly to lrx/lry), whereas IIIF defines top-left origin plus width and height.

answer.text: TEI coordinates are measured in inches, while IIIF coordinates are measured in millimeters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both systems use unitless integer coordinates in their respective canvas spaces.

answer.text: TEI places the origin (0,0) at the bottom-right, while IIIF places it in the exact center.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both conventions place the coordinate origin (0,0) at the top-left corner.

answer.text: TEI coordinates must always be prime numbers, whereas IIIF requires powers of two.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coordinates in both formats are arbitrary integers representing spatial bounds.

name.text: 07 Question: Binding Transcription to Zones with @facs

questiontext.text: In a TEI document, how does a line beginning element (<lb>) link to its corresponding physical region on the manuscript?

generalfeedback.text: @facs on and binds transcription to zones; declare zones locally so coordinates can be corrected in one place.

answer.text: It uses the @facs attribute containing a fragment reference (e.g., facs="#f42r_l01") pointing to the xml:id of a declared <zone> element.

feedback.text: Correct. points to the declared in the header.

answer.text: It embeds a base64-encoded JPEG image directly inside the <lb> element text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. is an empty milestone element linking via @facs, not embedding binary data.

answer.text: It uses a CSS class selector that fetches random image tiles from search engines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @facs resolves to explicit XML zone identifiers within the document or external canvas URIs.

answer.text: It executes a JavaScript fetch() command that modifies the remote TEI schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is declarative XML markup; @facs is an attribute expressing an ID reference.

name.text: 08 Question: Connecting surface to the IIIF Canvas

questiontext.text: How does a TEI <surface> element establish a bidirectional link to a IIIF Presentation API Canvas?

generalfeedback.text: Put the canvas URI on and record dimensions at every level, so coordinate mismatches can be detected rather than silently misplacing regions.

answer.text: By declaring the full canvas URI in its @facs attribute (e.g., facs="https://.../canvas/p42") and recording surface dimensions in ulx, uly, lrx, lry.

feedback.text: Correct. The carries the external canvas URI in @facs and defines the surface coordinate bounds in its attributes.

answer.text: By attaching a PDF copy of the manuscript to the TEI document via an email attachment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The link is established through web URIs in the @facs attribute.

answer.text: By embedding the library's SQL database username and password in <surface>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Public canvas URIs require no database credentials.

answer.text: By requiring all users to install a proprietary desktop font before opening the file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The connection is a standard web identifier link between XML and JSON-LD.

name.text: 09 Question: Generating the Fragment URI

questiontext.text: Given a <surface facs="https://.../canvas/p42"> and a child <zone xml:id="l01" ulx="420" uly="512" lrx="2580" lry="640"/>, what is the resulting IIIF fragment URI for line 1?

generalfeedback.text: Verify every binding by constructing the Image API URL for its region and confirming the returned image shows what you expected.

answer.text: https://.../canvas/p42#xywh=420,512,2160,128

feedback.text: Correct. Width is 2580 - 420 = 2160 and height is 640 - 512 = 128, yielding #xywh=420,512,2160,128 appended to the canvas URI.

answer.text: https://.../canvas/p42#xywh=420,512,2580,640

feedback.text: Incorrect. This mistakenly copies lrx and lry directly as width and height without subtracting ulx and uly.

answer.text: https://.../canvas/p42#corners=420,512,2160,128

feedback.text: Incorrect. The IIIF media fragment selector syntax uses #xywh=, not #corners=.

answer.text: https://.../canvas/p42/crop/420/512/2580/640

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is an invalid URL structure; IIIF fragment selectors use standard #xywh= syntax on canvas URIs.

name.text: 10 Question: Authoring a Manifest: The Skeleton

questiontext.text: Why is generating a IIIF manifest using a Python script preferable to hand-editing the JSON file?

generalfeedback.text: Generate manifests from a script rather than hand-editing JSON, and commit the generator alongside its output.

answer.text: A script enforces correct JSON-LD structure, generates language maps, formats required metadata consistently, and enables reproducible regeneration.

feedback.text: Correct. Scripting prevents recurring syntax mistakes (trailing commas, string labels vs. language maps) and ensures reproducibility.

answer.text: Hand-edited JSON files are automatically deleted by the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-edited files are valid if syntax is correct, but prone to human authoring errors.

answer.text: Python scripts are the only software licensed to output Unicode Greek characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any text editor can write Unicode Greek; scripts automate structural consistency.

answer.text: IIIF validators reject manifests that were not compiled by Python 3.12.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validators evaluate JSON-LD syntax and schema compliance regardless of how the file was generated.

name.text: 11 Question: Authoring a Manifest: Canvases

questiontext.text: In a Presentation API 3.0 manifest, what is the consequence of omitting the service block inside an image body?

generalfeedback.text: Include the service block or deep zoom will not work, and set canvas dimensions from the image's own dimensions.

answer.text: The viewer treats the image as a single static file and cannot request multi-resolution tiles, degrading deep zoom to client-side image scaling.

feedback.text: Correct. The service block informs the viewer of the Image API service endpoint needed for dynamic deep zoom tiling.

answer.text: The viewer will invert the colors of the manuscript, turning black ink white.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omission of the service block disables dynamic tiling; it does not invert pixel colors.

answer.text: The web browser will permanently block all network traffic to the domain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The image will simply be loaded as a static file without deep zoom capability.

answer.text: The manifest file will fail JSON syntax parsing with a fatal error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The JSON remains syntactically valid, but lacks the image service description for deep zoom.

name.text: 12 Question: Adding a Choice for Spectral Layers

questiontext.text: When constructing a Choice body for alternative spectral layers on a canvas, what should the first entry in the items array represent?

generalfeedback.text: A Choice expresses spectral alternatives on one canvas, and its labels must state the imaging conditions precisely enough to be evaluated.

answer.text: The natural visible-colour image, because viewers display the first item in the Choice list by default.

feedback.text: Correct. The initial item in a Choice list is the default display layer in viewers like Mirador.

answer.text: An uncalibrated high-noise PCA component to test viewer rendering speed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The default view should be the standard natural-colour image for baseline reading.

answer.text: A blank transparent PNG file to obscure the manuscript from unauthorized viewers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Choice layers present real alternative imaging captures for scholarly use.

answer.text: The institutional library's logo in vector SVG format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Choice items must be image layers of the physical manuscript folio.

name.text: 13 Question: Ranges: Identifying Your Passage Within the Codex

questiontext.text: Why is using a IIIF Range preferable to publishing an extracted passage as a standalone, disconnected manifest?

generalfeedback.text: A range identifies your passage within the full codex rather than detaching it, preserving the codicological context as part of the edition.

answer.text: A Range identifies the passage's constituent canvases within the codex's full sequence, preserving codicological context as scholarly evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Ranges allow navigation directly to a passage while maintaining its structural place within the complete manuscript.

answer.text: Standalone manifests are forbidden under the IIIF specification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standalone manifests are syntactically legal, but isolate the passage from its codicological context.

answer.text: Ranges automatically encrypt the rest of the manuscript to prevent unauthorized browsing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ranges provide table-of-contents navigation across open canvases.

answer.text: A Range converts medieval Greek script into modern German prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ranges define structural groupings of canvases, not textual translations.

name.text: 14 Question: Validating What You Have Built

questiontext.text: Why is structural schema validation alone insufficient to ensure a IIIF manifest and its TEI bindings are correct?

generalfeedback.text: Validators check structure, not meaning — a conformant manifest can have every coordinate wrong, so verify regions visually.

answer.text: Validators check syntax and schema conformance, but cannot detect whether coordinates point to the wrong lines or whether remote image URLs resolve.

feedback.text: Correct. A manifest can pass all schema validators while pointing to moved images or misplaced coordinates; visual checking is required.

answer.text: Schema validators only run on Windows operating systems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validators run across all platforms; their limitation is checking form rather than empirical accuracy.

answer.text: Schema validators intentionally insert random coordinates into XML documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validators are deterministic checking tools.

answer.text: Validating TEI documents invalidates the accompanying Git repository history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation checks files without affecting version control history.

name.text: 15 Question: Preparing for HTR Ingestion

questiontext.text: Why must a custom IIIF manifest be published at an HTTP/HTTPS URL rather than remaining as a local file before Week 4?

generalfeedback.text: HTR platforms fetch manifests over HTTP, so a manifest that exists only as a local file cannot be ingested.

answer.text: HTR platforms (like Transkribus or eScriptorium) fetch images by dereferencing the manifest URL over the public web during ingestion.

feedback.text: Correct. Remote cloud HTR platforms require public HTTP/HTTPS endpoints to fetch manifests and image tiles.

answer.text: Local JSON files are automatically erased by Git upon commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks local files normally; the constraint is remote platform web accessibility.

answer.text: Local files cannot store numbers larger than 1000.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File systems handle arbitrary data; HTR servers simply cannot access private local paths.

answer.text: The IIIF specification requires manifests to be stored exclusively on government servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests can be hosted on any web server, such as GitHub Pages.

name.text: 16 Question: From ALTO to TEI: What Next Week Produces

questiontext.text: How do the spatial coordinates emitted in ALTO/PAGE XML by HTR platforms relate to TEI <zone> elements?

generalfeedback.text: ALTO coordinates are in image pixels, so today's hand-verified zones are the control that will catch a scaling error in next week's transform.

answer.text: ALTO outputs bounding boxes in image pixel coordinates, which correspond structurally to TEI zones but may require scaling if canvas dimensions differ from image pixels.

feedback.text: Correct. ALTO boxes map directly to TEI zones, requiring coordinate scaling if canvas and image spaces diverge.

answer.text: ALTO coordinates are expressed in degrees of latitude and longitude.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO uses 2D raster pixel bounding boxes.

answer.text: ALTO XML does not record any spatial coordinates or line positions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO is an established spatial standard recording bounding boxes and baselines.

answer.text: TEI zones cannot accept numeric coordinates from automated OCR/HTR tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI attributes (ulx, uly, lrx, lry) specifically store geometric coordinates.

name.text: 17 Question: What Belongs in the Repository

questiontext.text: Why should manifest generator scripts (e.g., build_manifest.py) and source documentation (SOURCES.md) be committed alongside generated JSON files?

generalfeedback.text: Commit generators alongside generated files, and record external resources as documents because they change without notice.

answer.text: Committing generators and documentation ensures reproducibility, explaining how data was constructed and preserving external endpoint records against link rot.

feedback.text: Correct. Generators and source records make the digital edition fully auditable, reproducible, and resilient over time.

answer.text: Git repositories fail to push if they contain only JSON files without Python code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks any file type; the rule ensures scholarly auditability and reproducibility.

answer.text: Committing Python scripts prevents external researchers from viewing the JSON files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version-controlled scripts document the transformation pipeline openly.

answer.text: Generator scripts automatically delete compiled editions after thirty days.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scripts provide permanent, reproducible build instructions.

name.text: 18 Question: The Cataloguing and Metadata Assignment

questiontext.text: In the Cataloguing and Metadata Assignment, what is evaluated alongside the correctness of the TEI header and image bindings?

generalfeedback.text: The commit history is assessed alongside the content, and an invalid TEI header is the most common avoidable failure.

answer.text: The Git commit history, which must demonstrate atomic, typed commits with informative rationale explaining editorial decisions.

feedback.text: Correct. The version-controlled process record is an assessed deliverable alongside the TEI and metadata content.

answer.text: The speed at which the student typed their transcription in words per minute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Typing speed is irrelevant; structural accuracy and process rationale are assessed.

answer.text: Whether the student purchased a commercial font licence for their edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course uses open standards and open-source tooling.

answer.text: The physical weight of the student's computer hardware.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Assessment focuses on scholarly encoding, metadata, and version control discipline.

name.text: 19 Question: Common Errors in Today's Work

questiontext.text: If every bounding box on a folio is shifted and scaled by an identical ratio, what is the root cause?

generalfeedback.text: A scaling error makes every binding wrong by the same ratio, so it looks internally consistent — only visual comparison catches it.

answer.text: A scaling discrepancy between canvas coordinate dimensions and master image pixel dimensions that was not corrected during coordinate conversion.

feedback.text: Correct. A constant ratio error across all zones indicates a failure to scale image pixel coordinates to canvas dimensions.

answer.text: The medieval scribe used a crooked ruler when drawing ink guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribal ruling variations are local physical irregularities, not systematic digital scaling ratios.

answer.text: The web browser is running low on battery power, causing pixel compression.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Battery levels have no effect on mathematical coordinate rendering in browsers.

answer.text: The XML document contains a typo in its root <TEI> namespace tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Namespace typos cause schema validation failures, not proportional coordinate scaling offsets.

name.text: 20 Question: Exercise: Build the Binding

questiontext.text: Why is hand-verifying three lines of transcription coordinates more valuable today than generating three hundred unverified line coordinates?

generalfeedback.text: Three verified lines are worth more than three hundred unverified ones — the point is a control you understand.

answer.text: Three hand-verified lines provide an understood, reliable baseline to calibrate and debug next week's automated HTR coordinate transformation.

feedback.text: Correct. A carefully verified small control set allows rapid detection and correction of systematic pipeline errors.

answer.text: TEI schemas reject documents that contain more than three lines of text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI documents can contain millions of lines; the limitation today is pedagogical focus on verification.

answer.text: Three lines is the maximum amount of text that can fit in a single Git commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git commits can store arbitrarily large files.

answer.text: Hand measurement takes 24 hours per line, making larger samples physically impossible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand measurement takes seconds, but establishing a verified control is the primary objective.

name.text: 21 Question: Bidirectionality and What It Enables

questiontext.text: How does bidirectional coordinate binding streamline Week 5's transcription reconciliation phase?

generalfeedback.text: The binding makes verification cheap, and cheap verification is verification that actually happens.

answer.text: An editor can click directly between disputed readings in the text and the corresponding manuscript image region instantly, making verification rapid and routine.

feedback.text: Correct. Direct spatial jumping allows editors to check ground truth against HTR output in seconds rather than hunting through facsimiles.

answer.text: It allows the computer to automatically overwrite the manuscript image with modern Greek typography.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The binding creates navigable links between transcription and original images.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for human editors to review transcription errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Bidirectional navigation empowers human editors to reconcile readings efficiently.

answer.text: It translates the manuscript into Latin, Hebrew, and Syriac simultaneously.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spatial binding connects transcription to image coordinates.

name.text: 22 Question: Coordinate Stability Over the Term

questiontext.text: What is the most effective safeguard against institutional image rescans that change canvas dimensions later in the term?

generalfeedback.text: Record the canvas dimensions your coordinates were computed against, because a rescan invalidates them silently.

answer.text: Record the original canvas dimensions alongside your coordinates and document access dates, allowing a mathematical correction factor to be computed if dimensions change.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording baseline dimensions and access dates enables systematic recalculation if an institution republishes at different dimensions.

answer.text: Store all coordinates exclusively in handwritten paper notebooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital reproducibility requires version-controlled records in the repository.

answer.text: Disable all internet connections on your computer until December.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital scholarship requires web connectivity; recording baseline metadata safeguards against changes.

answer.text: Request that the holding library freeze all digitization activities worldwide.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Libraries update digital holdings independently; defensive documentation is the editor's responsibility.

name.text: 23 Question: Looking Ahead: Week 4 and the Three-Step Cycle

questiontext.text: What role does Tuesday's manual diplomatic transcription play in the course's three-step comparative cycle?

generalfeedback.text: Tuesday's manual transcription is the ground truth that every later measurement depends on, and today's binding is what makes transcribing accurately affordable.

answer.text: It establishes the verified human ground truth against which deterministic HTR (Wednesday) and AI-assisted transcription (Friday) are objectively evaluated.

feedback.text: Correct. The manual diplomatic transcription serves as the baseline ground truth for measuring HTR and LLM error rates in Week 5.

answer.text: It serves as a rough, disposable draft that will be deleted once AI models run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual transcription is the gold-standard ground truth for the entire course.

answer.text: It is an optional exercise that can be skipped if automated OCR passes without syntax errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Establishing human ground truth is mandatory for comparative evaluation.

answer.text: It generates the final published critical commentary automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary is authored in Week 12 based on the verified edition.

name.text: 24 Question: Publishing the Manifest

questiontext.text: When publishing a custom manifest via GitHub Pages, what two technical requirements must be satisfied for external IIIF viewers to load it?

generalfeedback.text: The manifest's id must equal its actual URL, and CORS must permit cross-origin loading or only your own machine can use it.

answer.text: The manifest's declared id must match its public URL, and the server must provide permissive Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) headers.

feedback.text: Correct. IIIF requires matching dereferenceable id URLs and CORS headers to allow cross-domain viewer loading.

answer.text: The manifest must be password-protected and encrypted with a 4096-bit RSA key.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Public IIIF manifests must be accessible without authentication or private encryption.

answer.text: The repository must be written in assembly language and hosted on a physical mainframe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub Pages provides standard static HTTPS hosting for JSON-LD files.

answer.text: The manifest must be converted into a PDF document before publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests must remain valid JSON-LD files.

name.text: 25 Question: The Week in the Arc of the Course

questiontext.text: How does the infrastructure built in Week 3 (IIIF manifests, canvases, and coordinate bindings) support the remaining weeks of the course?

generalfeedback.text: Nearly every remaining layer of the edition attaches to the canvas coordinate space built this week.

answer.text: It provides the unified spatial coordinate spine to which transcription, normalization, collation, apparatus, and commentary all attach.

feedback.text: Correct. Every subsequent layer of the digital edition anchors directly to the canvas coordinate space established this week.

answer.text: It completes all course work, making the remaining ten weeks unnecessary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 3 establishes the imaging foundation; the edition itself is constructed in Weeks 4 through 13.

answer.text: It replaces the TEI XML guidelines with an image-only photo album.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI text and IIIF images are bound together into an integrated digital edition.

answer.text: It restricts all subsequent work strictly to printing physical paper facsimiles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The infrastructure enables interactive digital publication and analysis.

name.text: 26 Question: Interoperability as a Scholarly Value

questiontext.text: In what way is technical interoperability (IIIF/TEI) analogous to traditional scholarly apparatus conventions (sigla, apparatus criticus)?

generalfeedback.text: Standards let scholars cooperate without coordinating, and an edition that only its author can use is not yet scholarship.

answer.text: Both are standardized conventions that allow independent scholars to communicate, compare, and verify evidence without requiring prior bilateral coordination.

feedback.text: Correct. Standardized protocols and critical sigla both enable collaboration and verification without bilateral negotiation.

answer.text: Both were invented in the twenty-first century by commercial software corporations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Critical apparatus conventions evolved over centuries of classical philology.

answer.text: Both are designed to restrict manuscript reading exclusively to tenured university professors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open standards democratize access and enable transparent scholarly communication.

answer.text: Both require specialized proprietary software licences that expire annually.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both represent open, enduring scholarly standards.

name.text: 27 Question: A Checklist Before You Leave

questiontext.text: Why is opening an Image API URL for a newly bound zone the most critical validation check before completing today's work?

generalfeedback.text: Verify zones by opening their Image API URLs — structural validation cannot tell you whether a coordinate is right.

answer.text: It provides direct visual verification that the computed coordinates actually frame the intended line of text on the manuscript page.

feedback.text: Correct. Visual inspection of the returned crop is the only test that verifies semantic correctness rather than mere syntax.

answer.text: It tests whether the student's monitor has sufficient brightness for reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It verifies the mathematical accuracy of the coordinate crop.

answer.text: It automatically registers the digital edition with the Library of Congress.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It confirms the URL returns the intended visual evidence.

answer.text: It verifies that the holding library has paid its annual web hosting bill.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It tests the validity of the specific coordinate binding.

name.text: 28 Question: If Your Manuscript Lacks IIIF

questiontext.text: If a chosen manuscript is available only as static image files without a native IIIF server, how can an editor still build a valid TEI edition?

generalfeedback.text: Without IIIF you can still bind coordinates using plain images and TEI zones — you lose deep zoom, not the binding the course depends on.

answer.text: Use standard TEI <graphic> and <zone> elements using pixel coordinates, or generate a static Level 0 IIIF tile pyramid with tools like iiif_static.py.

feedback.text: Correct. Editors can either bind TEI zones directly to static graphics or generate a Level 0 static tile pyramid for GitHub Pages.

answer.text: Abandon digital methods entirely and write the edition on parchment with a quill.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Valid TEI editions can be constructed using static graphics and standard zones.

answer.text: Sue the holding library for non-compliance with digital humanities standards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Practical workarounds (TEI graphic/zone or Level 0 static generation) handle non-IIIF sources.

answer.text: Delete the manuscript's catalogue record from global library databases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Non-IIIF images remain fully usable via standard TEI facsimile markup.

name.text: 29 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a high-quality scholarly submission from a minimally compliant one on the Cataloguing and Metadata Assignment?

generalfeedback.text: A good submission records divergences, negative results, and the reasoning behind decisions — not only what worked.

answer.text: A good submission documents editorial reasoning, notes divergences from library catalogues with rationale, records negative results, and maintains an atomic commit log.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly rigor is demonstrated by documenting rationale, divergences, image provenance, and negative results.

answer.text: A good submission has the largest file size measured in gigabytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Quality is measured by scholarly documentation, accuracy, and rationale, not raw file size.

answer.text: A good submission must be translated into at least seven modern European languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The assignment focuses on Greek transcription, metadata, and image binding.

answer.text: A good submission conceals all difficulties, uncertainties, and failed attempts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transparent recording of uncertainties and negative results is a hallmark of good scholarship.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Coordinate Space as the Edition's Spine

questiontext.text: Why is the canvas coordinate space described as the 'spine' of the digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: The canvas coordinate space is the spine of the edition; every layer from transcription to commentary attaches to it, which is what makes them one object.

answer.text: Every subsequent analytical layer — transcription, apparatus, collation, linguistic annotation, commentary — anchors to its coordinates, uniting them into a single object.

feedback.text: Correct. The canvas coordinate space provides the unifying framework that integrates images, transcription, apparatus, and commentary.

answer.text: It binds the printed paper pages of the final codex with synthetic bookbinding glue.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Spine' is the structural metaphor for the digital coordinate space uniting all edition layers.

answer.text: It encrypts the entire repository into a closed proprietary database format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The spine is an open coordinate system connecting open TEI and IIIF standards.

answer.text: It automatically corrects all historical scribal spelling errors without human intervention.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The coordinate space anchors human scholarly analysis and evidence.
